evals.prompt: We're releasing a change to our public Go client library that alters the default timeout behavior consumers have been observably relying on for retries, and the team wants to ship it as a PATCH version bump (e.g. 1.4.2 -> 1.4.3). Is that the right version bump?
evals.expected_output: Flags that a behavior change consumers observably relied on is a breaking change regardless of how small the diff looks, and recommends a MAJOR version bump instead of a patch.

assertions.text: Flags this as a breaking change, not a patch

evals.prompt: We're releasing a breaking v2.0.0 of our Go module `github.com/archipelago/sentec-client`, and just pushed the git tag `v2.0.0` without changing anything in go.mod. Will consumers be able to correctly get this new major version via `go get`?
evals.expected_output: Flags that Go modules require the major version to be reflected in the module's import path (e.g. module github.com/archipelago/sentec-client/v2) for v2 and above, and that just tagging v2.0.0 without updating go.mod's module path will not resolve correctly for consumers.

assertions.text: Flags the missing /v2 import path change in go.mod
States this will cause a resolution problem for consumers

evals.prompt: We have one giant commit containing a refactor, a new feature, and a bug fix all mixed together, and now we're trying to use git bisect to find which change introduced a regression. Why is this hard, and what should we do differently going forward?
evals.expected_output: Explains that git bisect works best with atomic commits that each do one logical thing, and a mixed commit makes it ambiguous which part caused the regression; recommends committing each logical change separately going forward.

assertions.text: Explains the ambiguity problem for bisect with mixed commits
